speakers: Alan (host, sitting in for Niels Kaastrup-Larsen)
summary: Systematic Investor 315: Cham argues year-end rebalancing, dealer skew and holiday-volume flows make Oct 2024 to mid-January bullish, then expects a blow-off top. Macro view is structural/populist inflation (stagflation decade), steepeners, and election scenarios (Trump vs Harris) with China as a tactical trade.

coverage.note: CTA recap, vol compression and cheap long-dated calls
outlook to early next year, wall of worry, seasonality is structural flows
year-end rebalancing and releveraging mechanics, size of flows
mid-Dec to mid-Jan seasonality, holiday volume-time, expirations
election skew and dealer flows, blow-off top risk
China stimulus, mean reversion of neglected markets
rule-of-law failures, China as tactical trade

40-year deflation regime to populist inflation regime

China timing by candidate, oil, immigration

sugar high, blow-off tops, early warnings, outro

claims.speaker: Alan (host)
claims.quote: the ongoing rally in equities, uh uh gains in bonds, um weakness in the dollar, uh and and the down move in oil all relevant in in the trend-following world
claims.claim: Trend-following indices were up about 1.4% in the month and 2.7% year to date, driven by the equity rally, bond gains, a weaker dollar and lower oil.
claims.direction: trend followers long equities and bonds, short dollar and oil
claims.testable: partly: index returns are public but this is a one-month description

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: as tends to happen when you get a decent-size rally relative to a short amount of time, the vol compression gets overdone
claims.claim: After a fast rally implied vol gets compressed too far, so long-dated calls become cheap.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 implied vol, long-dated OTM calls vs ATM
claims.conditions: after a quick rally with event risk ahead
claims.testable: yes: compare implied vol to long-run average after rallies

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: we're talking about a sub-sub-10 uh vol in the S&P 500
claims.claim: S&P 500 vol was priced under 10 versus a long-run at-the-money average near 17.5, which Cham reads as very cheap given geopolitics and the election.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 implied vol vs 17.5 long-term average
claims.testable: yes: threshold on implied vol relative to long-run mean

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: I would argue the highest probability, if you look forward into from now into early next year, so next 3 and 1/2 months or so, is for us to go higher
claims.claim: Cham expects equities to rise into early next year and long-dated vol to rise on a fixed-strike basis even if the VIX stays flat.
claims.testable: partly: view with a specific window

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: We like to think of it as a releveraging. The world keeps risk neutral.
claims.claim: The wealth effect is better described as releveraging: institutions hold risk constant, so higher asset values force them to add exposure.
claims.testable: partly: needs a measurable proxy for institutional rebalancing

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: And that high skew is something that people call the wall of worry broadly.
claims.claim: High equity skew in Nov-Jan drives vol-and-time (vanna/charm) hedge unwinds by dealers, which supports prices; this is the real content of the wall of worry.
claims.conditions: when skew is high going into year end
claims.testable: yes: condition on skew level and test forward returns

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: There are actually big structural factors that are consistent and reliable that create higher probability outcomes during different periods of the year.
claims.claim: Seasonality is not psychology (Santa Claus rally) but structural flows tied to rebalancing, expirations and holiday volume.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: some major effects do fall at the end and beginning of months
claims.claim: Some structural flow effects fall at month-end and month-start and others in mid-month tied to option expiration cycles.
claims.testable: yes: turn-of-month and OPEX effects are testable

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: most asset managers and the most institutions manage capital, including banks, is they invest risk neutral
claims.claim: A 20% equity rise adds about $50 trillion of collateral across roughly $250 trillion of equity-linked assets, and institutions must reinvest it to keep risk constant, creating buying.
claims.indicator: global equity market value, year-to-date return
claims.direction: buy equities after large up years into year end
claims.testable: partly: flow size is an estimate

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: call it about 10%, um, comes in on January 1st
claims.claim: About 10% of the new equity-linked capital (about $5 trillion) is reinvested on January 1 by slower institutions such as private equity and real estate.
claims.direction: long equities around the turn of the year
claims.testable: partly: the 10% is a rough guess

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: On your average day, it's actually about 100 billion dollars that moves markets
claims.claim: Only about $100 billion trades on an average day, so a $5 trillion reinvestment is about 20 times normal daily volume and floats are tiny relative to market cap.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: it's actually the middle of December to the middle of January.
claims.claim: The strongest four-week seasonal window of the year over 125 years is mid-December to mid-January (Santa rally plus January effect), with almost all gains coming in up years.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 seasonal returns mid-Dec to mid-Jan
claims.conditions: mainly in years when the market was up

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: Where people have to chase and that chase matters.
claims.claim: Everyone sees the year-end rebalancing coming, and year-end performance reporting forces underinvested managers to chase, creating a cascade.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: removes risk more quickly from the market and drives a ton of buyback of tail
claims.claim: Holidays from Thanksgiving to early January cut volume-weighted time, which speeds vol decay and charm flows so dealers buy back tail hedges and the market is lifted.
claims.indicator: volume-weighted time, charm flows, holiday calendar
claims.direction: long equities from Thanksgiving to early January
claims.testable: partly: structural argument, testable via seasonal returns

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: the biggest expirations for structured products, options, all kinds of other risk products that manage the tail are December and January
claims.claim: The largest expirations of structured products and tail hedges (index options in December, single stocks in early January) add to the late-year hedge unwinding.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: What that means is dealers are short puts on a very high price with a very high delta and are short stock, typically.
claims.claim: With elevated skew into the election, dealers are short expensive puts and short stock, so as skew decays and time passes they must buy back stock, creating a tidal wave of positive flows.
claims.conditions: when skew is elevated and then collapses

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: If we were to lose 20% of the market, we would lose all those positive flows at the end of the year
claims.claim: The flow-driven rally has a fat left tail: a 20% fall around the election would remove the year-end reinvestment flows and could accelerate the decline.
claims.conditions: if a large decline occurs before year end

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: and that also will drive positive flows regardless of who gets elected, those flows will come into the market
claims.claim: Election events carry skew that, once resolved, drives positive flows whoever wins.
claims.testable: yes: post-election returns across election cycles

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: this is also a perfect setup for for a blow-off top for for long positions
claims.claim: Strong year-end flows are bullish only until January 13-15, and the same set-up is a classic blow-off top, so Cham holds a bullish flows view alongside a bearish macro view.
claims.direction: long into January, then risk of a top

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: it starts moving up as a broad structured trade that's one of the worst times to try and short
claims.claim: When a long-neglected market starts rising off the bottom, shorting it is especially dangerous; Cham prefers exposure, as in China after the stimulus.
claims.conditions: after a policy-driven rebound from depressed levels
claims.testable: partly: depends on how bottom is defined

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: works really well or 90% of scenarios I would say
claims.claim: Going long a market that has underperformed for 3-5 years and starts to mean revert works in about 85-90% of cases and tends to run for years.
claims.indicator: multi-year relative valuation and performance gap
claims.direction: long the cheap, long-underperforming market vs the expensive one

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: There's a bigger structural issue that that makes people unwilling to invest
claims.claim: The failures of the mean reversion trade (Russia, Iran, arguably Japan) share a rule-of-law/property-rights problem that stops investors returning regardless of valuation.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: no amount of the valuation gap is really going to close that difference
claims.claim: The US-China bifurcation means China may suffer from the same structural investability problem, so cheap valuation alone will not close the gap with the West.
claims.direction: cautious on Chinese equities long term

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: So it's something to play with calls, with leverage, with limited downside.
claims.claim: Cham sees the China stimulus rally as a tactical trade into December-January, best expressed with calls and limited downside, not as an investment.
claims.conditions: until January and subject to the election outcome
claims.testable: partly: instrument choice, view is time bound

claims.speaker: Alan (host)
claims.quote: it's still kind of uh you know, it's not coming down anymore
claims.claim: Core PCE year-on-year was stuck near 2.7% even as the Fed message shifted to labor market downside risk.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: when uh inflation cyclically is declining is exactly the moment uh that we start to see a counterintuitive steepener starts to happen
claims.claim: When cyclical inflation falls and the Fed eases, the long end of the curve sells off (a bear steepener) because investors price structural inflation returning.
claims.conditions: when cyclical disinflation coincides with structural inflation
claims.testable: yes: curve slope after first cut across cycles

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: There are two things that drive inflation, right? There's just business cycle, right?
claims.claim: Inflation has a cyclical component (business cycle) and a secular component (policy regime), and for 40 years only the cyclical one mattered.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: That's the cycle we were in for 40 years, a massive deflationary cycle driven by technological development, globalization broadly, and incredibly low interest rates
claims.claim: The 40-year deflationary era came from easy money flowing to the top, globalization, technology and low rates, and it produced record corporate margins and inequality.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: It leads to global conflict. It leads to scarcity of resources and hoarding of resources
claims.claim: Inequality gives populist politics that favor fiscal demand-push, redistribution, deglobalization, conflict and resource hoarding, a secular inflation regime like the 1970s.
claims.direction: long real assets, short long bonds

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: Under the hood, you're they're battling structural inflation with cyclical pressures.
claims.claim: Rate hikes slow the economy and cool inflation temporarily, as in the 60s and 70s, but do not remove the structural inflation, so it returns.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: What it does is it sequesters demand.
claims.claim: Interest rate effects are non-linear: high rates hold back demand (e.g. home purchases) that is released inelastically once rates fall, so rate cuts re-accelerate the economy.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: all of a sudden the the economy re-accelerated
claims.claim: After the Fed's December 2023 pivot, the feared bad news did not arrive; pent-up demand returned as the 10-year fell and the economy re-accelerated.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: I think we're on transitory 4.0 now.
claims.claim: Cham expects a persistently hot demand-push economy, with repeated 'transitory' episodes until the long end of the curve stops believing it.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: and we believe you're in a decade of stagflation here going forward
claims.claim: The Fed will be forced back into a box of slow growth and structural inflation, a decade of stagflation, which is harder to manage than deflationary pressure.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: the best way to play that is to continue to play the steepener
claims.claim: Every Fed cut should steepen the curve because it feeds longer-term inflation expectations while lowering the front end, so Cham stays in curve steepeners.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: the trade we were looking for and we've talked about now for nine nine to 69 months and it's it's not playing out.
claims.claim: The steepener thesis had been held for many months without paying off, and Cham reads that as part of the structural story rather than a failure.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: the Treasury's going to continue to be as uh as supportive as possible until the election
claims.claim: Treasury is expected to stay supportive (bill-heavy issuance) up to the election, with incentives to prioritize short-term results.
claims.indicator: Treasury refunding (Oct 30), bill vs coupon issuance

claims.speaker: Alan (host)
claims.quote: we had this spike in yields kind of from August to October around concerns about um refinancing the debt and uh debt sustainability
claims.claim: Last year yields spiked from August to October on debt sustainability concerns before Treasury shifted issuance toward bills.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: why election years are so positive in general
claims.claim: Governments have an incentive to make the short term look good in election years, which supports markets.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: The biggest issues are fiscal policy, global conflict, labor costs and protectionism, right? And then commodity and input prices.
claims.claim: Structural inflation is driven by fiscal policy, global conflict, labor costs/protectionism and commodity prices, so Cham assesses candidates on these.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: I think that creates a massive cyclical positive for markets in the short term, but also drives a much worse structural secular inflation pressure.
claims.claim: A Trump win would be stimulative with pressure on the Fed (Nixon/Erdogan analogy): a big short-term market positive but worse structural inflation.
claims.direction: long equities near term, short long bonds

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: it is inflationary. It's something that can be uh very stagflationary
claims.claim: A Harris win means redistribution via capital gains tax and is more measured, but still inflationary and possibly worse for markets near term.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: the odds of China moving in some form or other against Taiwan is high as about as high as 50% in the next 4 years
claims.claim: Cham puts about a 50% chance on Chinese action against Taiwan within four years and links it to Russia and Iran as one structured movement.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: Think of it as the eye of a storm where uh everybody's in a holding pattern.
claims.claim: Countries and corporations are holding off big moves until the US election result is known, so geopolitical actions may follow the result.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: a much higher probability of a Trump presidency leading to a quicker, more abrupt action
claims.claim: Under Trump China's move would come sooner and resolve sooner, possibly leading to a detente and a rally in Chinese assets; under Harris it is later and longer.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: I believe there is a higher chance of Trump making a deal with Saudi, uh giving guarantees on security
claims.claim: A Saudi deal under Trump could offset energy-driven inflation from stimulus, while rising energy costs hurt Europe and Japan.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: I think the one thing that has been holding down labor inflation in the US relative to how bad it could have been given the de-globalization everything we're seeing is massive immigration.
claims.claim: Strong immigration has held down US labor inflation, so hardline restriction would be structurally inflationary.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: If Trump wins, he likely wins both houses, even though it's a very close election.
claims.claim: The House has never swung without the presidential candidate winning and Democrats can only hold the Senate with a Harris VP tie-break, so a Trump win means a united government and bigger moves.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: those periods are very bad for equities and bonds.
claims.claim: Inflationary populist regimes hurt both equities and bonds: the last 14-year period of rising rates lost about 70% in real terms, so 60/40 suffers.
claims.indicator: real equity and bond returns in rising rate regimes

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: The average performance is 21%. Every single one is up double digits.
claims.claim: In populist election years the market averaged +21% with a 100% win rate, versus about +5% for all other elections since 1928, on stimulus to win the vote.
claims.indicator: election-year S&P return, populist election years

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: So, the last thing you want to do is after that election year go in long in the markets.
claims.claim: After populist election years the stimulus fades and markets mean revert and can retrace, so being long after the election is dangerous.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: I don't remember one bigger decline that didn't come with a rally
claims.claim: Large declines are preceded by blow-off rallies (2006 vs 2008 housing, 1999 tech then -92%), so the current rally could be a sugar high with the earliest top around January.

claims.speaker: Cham
claims.quote: it usually takes way longer than you expect
claims.claim: Warning signs usually play out later than expected because shorts and structural support keep the market going until something unsustainable occurs, so early bearish calls are costly.
